paragraphs: So far I have examined the institutions of the United States. I have reviewed their legislation, and I have described the present characteristics of political society in that country. But above these institutions and beyond these characteristic features there is a sovereign power that can destroy or change them as it pleases. I mean the power of the people. It remains to show how this power, which regulates the laws, acts. I must point out its inclinations and its passions, and the hidden springs that slow down, speed up, or direct its irresistible course. I must also show the effects of its unlimited authority and the destiny that probably awaits it.

In America the people appoints the legislative and the executive power, and supplies the jurors who punish every offense against the laws. American institutions are democratic not only in their principle but in all their consequences. The people elects its representatives directly, and for the most part annually, in order to keep them dependent on it. The people is therefore the real directing power. Although the form of government is representative, it is evident that the opinions, the prejudices, the interests, and even the passions of the community meet no lasting obstacle to their exercising a perpetual influence on society. In the United States the majority governs in the name of the people, as happens in every country where the people is supreme. The majority is composed mainly of peaceful citizens who, whether by inclination or by interest, sincerely desire the welfare of their country. But they are surrounded by the ceaseless agitation of parties, which try to win their cooperation and to make use of their support.
